questions.q: A BPE trainer finds two pairs tied for the highest count. Why does the tie-break rule matter?
options: Different merges give different vocabularies, so a fixed rule (such as lexicographic order) is needed for reproducible training
Both pairs are merged at once
The tie-break changes only the speed
questions.why: Without a deterministic rule, two runs on the same data can produce different tokenizers.

questions.q: Why do GPT-style tokenizers pre-split text with a regex before BPE?
options: To stop merges from crossing word, number or punctuation boundaries, such as "dog." becoming one token
questions.why: Pre-tokenisation keeps tokens meaningful and stops the vocabulary filling with variants of the same word plus punctuation.

questions.q: When encoding with a trained BPE, in what order are merges applied?
options: By the frequency of each pair in the input
By rank: repeatedly apply the lowest-ranked (earliest learned) merge present in the word
Left to right, greedily matching the longest token
questions.why: Applying merges in training order reproduces how the vocabulary was built.

questions.q: Why does byte-level BPE never need an unknown token?
options: It maps unknown text to spaces
It starts from the 256 byte values, so any string can be represented
questions.why: Rare characters become several byte tokens. The cost is longer sequences for non-Latin scripts.

questions.q: What does a larger vocabulary trade off?
options: Shorter sequences against a larger embedding and output layer, with rarer tokens seen less often in training
questions.why: The output softmax over V entries is a noticeable cost for small models with large vocabularies.

questions.q: Why are special tokens like `<|endoftext|>` handled outside of BPE merges?
options: They must map to a single reserved ID and never be produced by merging ordinary text
They are too long to merge
questions.why: Encoders split them out first, so user text containing the same characters can't inject control tokens by accident.

questions.q: The word "lower" is encoded with merges ranked (l,o) = 0, (lo,w) = 1, (e,r) = 2. What is the result?
questions.why: Apply (l,o) → "lo", then (lo,w) → "low", then (e,r) → "er". No further merges apply.

questions.q: Why should a tokenizer round-trip decode(encode(text)) == text?
options: Any loss means the model can't reproduce some inputs exactly, which breaks code, whitespace and evaluation
It is only needed for English
questions.why: Byte-level BPE gives exact round trips. Normalising tokenizers can lose information such as repeated spaces.

questions.q: What does `einsum('bhqd,bhkd->bhqk', q, k)` compute?
options: Attention scores for each batch and head: dot products between every query and every key
questions.why: The shared index d is summed over. The result has a q × k score matrix per batch and head.

questions.q: Why are named-dimension tools like einops useful in model code?
options: They remove the need for batching
They are faster than views in every case
Reshapes and transposes state their meaning explicitly, so axis mix-ups are easier to spot
questions.why: `rearrange(x, 'b t (h d) -> b h t d', h=heads)` is clearer than a chain of view and transpose calls.

questions.q: Training with AdamW in mixed precision, roughly how many bytes per parameter do weights, gradients and optimiser state take?
options: About 16: bf16 weights and grads (4), fp32 master weights (4) and two fp32 Adam moments (8)
questions.why: Activations come on top and depend on batch size and sequence length. This is why ZeRO-style sharding matters.

questions.q: What is the usual estimate of training FLOPs for a dense transformer?
questions.why: The forward pass is about 2N FLOPs per token and the backward pass about 4N. Attention adds a term that grows with context length.

questions.q: Why does gradient accumulation over k micro-batches give the same update as one batch k times larger?
options: It multiplies the learning rate by k
Each micro-batch updates the weights separately
It doesn't; the results always differ
Gradients are summed (or averaged) across micro-batches before the optimiser step, just as for one large batch
questions.why: Scale each micro-batch's loss by 1/k when the loss is a mean. Batch normalisation would break the equivalence, but transformers rarely use it.

questions.q: When does gradient accumulation fail to match a large batch exactly?
options: When the loss is averaged per micro-batch and micro-batches have different numbers of valid tokens
questions.why: Averaging per micro-batch weights tokens unequally. Summing losses and dividing by the total token count fixes it.

questions.q: What does `torch.no_grad()` do during evaluation?
options: Sets the model to eval mode
Stops autograd recording operations, saving memory and time
questions.why: Eval mode (`model.eval()`) is separate: it changes dropout and normalisation behaviour.

questions.q: Why is bf16 usually preferred over fp16 for training large models?
options: bf16 uses less memory than fp16
bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so it rarely overflows and doesn't need loss scaling
questions.why: bf16 keeps 8 exponent bits and drops mantissa bits. fp16 has more precision but a much smaller range.

questions.q: Why is RMSNorm cheaper than LayerNorm?
options: It skips mean subtraction and usually the bias, needing one reduction
questions.why: Empirically it performs about as well, which is why most recent LLMs use it.

questions.q: A SwiGLU FFN has three matrices instead of two. How is its hidden size usually set to match a standard FFN's parameters?
options: To about 2/3 of 4d, so 3 · d · (8d/3) ≈ 2 · d · 4d
questions.why: LLaMA used 2/3 · 4d rounded to a multiple of 256.

questions.q: In SwiGLU, what does the gate do?
options: Multiplies one projection element-wise by SiLU of another, letting the network control each hidden unit
questions.why: FFN(x) = W₂(SiLU(W₁x) ⊙ W₃x).

questions.q: Rotary embeddings make the score $q_m^\top k_n$ depend on what?
options: Only on the relative offset m − n (and the content of q and k)
questions.why: Rotating q by mθ and k by nθ gives a dot product that depends on (m − n)θ.

questions.q: Where is RoPE applied in an attention layer?
options: To queries and keys after projection, before the dot product; not to values
questions.why: Values carry content, not position, so they aren't rotated.

questions.q: What does a causal mask do in a decoder?
options: Sets scores for future positions to −∞ before the softmax so each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens
questions.why: It makes training on all positions at once equivalent to autoregressive prediction.

questions.q: In GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, how are keys used in the score computation?
options: Each query head gets its own key
Each KV head is shared by a group of 4 consecutive query heads (often by repeating it)
All query heads share one key
questions.why: Repeat-interleave or reshape the query heads into groups so no copy is made.

questions.q: Why do pre-norm transformers train more stably than post-norm ones at depth?
options: The residual path stays an identity, so gradients reach early layers without passing through normalisation each time
questions.why: Post-norm usually needs careful warm-up to train deep stacks.

questions.q: Linear attention replaces softmax with a feature map φ. What does that enable?
options: Computing $\phi(Q)(\phi(K)^\top V)$, which is linear in sequence length and can run as a recurrence
Exact softmax attention at lower cost
questions.why: With a causal mask, the running sum $S_t = S_{t-1} + \phi(k_t)v_t^\top$ is a fixed-size state.

questions.q: Why do the parallel and recurrent forms of causal linear attention give the same output?
options: The recurrent state is exactly the prefix sum of $\phi(k_i)v_i^\top$ that the masked parallel form computes
They don't; one approximates the other
The recurrent form ignores earlier tokens
questions.why: Training uses the parallel or chunked form; inference uses the recurrence with constant memory per token.

questions.q: What does a gating term add to a linear-attention state update, as in Mamba-2 or GLA?
options: A decay that lets the state forget old information at a learned, input-dependent rate
questions.why: $S_t = a_t S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^\top$. Without decay the state only accumulates and can't forget.

questions.q: The delta rule update $S_t = S_{t-1} + \beta_t(v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)k_t^\top$ does what?
options: Corrects the state toward storing $v_t$ under key $k_t$, overwriting what was stored there before
questions.why: It is one step of online regression for the key-value map. Gated DeltaNet multiplies $S_{t-1}$ by a decay first.

questions.q: Why are hybrid models often built with a few full attention layers among linear or state-space layers?
options: Recurrent layers have fixed-size memory and struggle with exact recall over long contexts; a few attention layers restore it
questions.why: The mix keeps most of the memory and speed benefits while recovering retrieval ability.

questions.q: A top-k MoE router computes what per token?
options: Scores for each expert; the top k are selected and their weights normalised
questions.why: Routers often use softmax or sigmoid scores. Selected weights may be renormalised to sum to 1.

questions.q: Which statistics does a router typically report for load balancing?
options: The fraction of tokens sent to each expert and the mean router probability per expert
questions.why: Their product summed over experts (times the number of experts) gives the standard auxiliary loss.

questions.q: What is the memory cost of a recurrent linear-attention layer at inference, per sequence?
options: A fixed d_k × d_v state per head, independent of context length
questions.why: Compare a KV cache, which grows by one key and value per token.

questions.q: What limits occupancy on a GPU streaming multiprocessor?
options: Registers per thread, shared memory per block, threads per block and the hardware's block and warp limits
questions.why: The most restrictive resource sets how many blocks fit on one SM at once.

questions.q: A kernel uses 64 registers per thread and the SM has 65,536 registers. What is the maximum number of resident threads by registers alone?
questions.why: 65,536 / 64 = 1,024. If the SM supports 2,048 threads, occupancy is capped at 50%.

questions.q: When do shared-memory bank conflicts happen?
options: When threads read the same address
When several threads in a warp access different addresses in the same bank in one instruction
When two warps use shared memory
questions.why: Shared memory has 32 banks of 4-byte words. Reading the same address broadcasts; different addresses in one bank are serialised.

questions.q: Threads in a warp read `smem[tid * 32]` (4-byte floats). How bad is the conflict?
questions.why: Bank = (address / 4) mod 32 = (tid · 32) mod 32 = 0. Padding the row length to 33 spreads them across banks.

questions.q: What does global memory coalescing mean?
options: A warp's accesses to consecutive addresses are combined into a few wide memory transactions
questions.why: Strided or scattered accesses need more transactions for the same useful bytes.

questions.q: A warp reads 32 floats with stride 2. Roughly how much of the fetched bandwidth is wasted?
questions.why: The warp touches 256 bytes of memory to use 128. Larger strides waste more.

questions.q: What is blockwise online softmax for?
options: Computing softmax over a long row in chunks with a running max and sum, without storing the row
questions.why: It is the core of FlashAttention.

questions.q: How does a TPU's matrix unit differ from a GPU's CUDA cores?
options: It is used only for inference
It is a large systolic array specialised for dense matmul, fed by the XLA compiler
questions.why: TPUs trade flexibility for very high matmul throughput, which is why kernels and sharding are planned by the compiler.

questions.q: In a masked Triton GELU kernel, what does the mask prevent?
options: Reads and writes past the end of the tensor in the last block
questions.why: `mask = offs < n` on both `tl.load` and `tl.store`.

questions.q: A Triton row-wise softmax with the whole row in one block does how many trips to global memory per element?
questions.why: Max, exponent, sum and divide happen on-chip.

questions.q: In a tiled row-sum kernel where rows are longer than the block, what does each program do?
options: Loops over its row in BLOCK-sized chunks, accumulating a partial sum, then writes one value
Writes a partial per chunk with no accumulation
questions.why: The loop keeps memory per program fixed whatever the row length.

questions.q: What is the benefit of fusing ReLU into a tiled matmul kernel?
options: It is applied to the accumulator in registers, avoiding a separate pass over the output
It doubles throughput of the matmul itself
It removes the need for tiling
questions.why: Epilogue fusion is close to free.

questions.q: What does XLA do with a JAX or TensorFlow computation graph?
options: Interprets each operation separately at runtime
Runs it on the CPU only
Compiles it as a whole, fusing operations and choosing layouts before generating device code
questions.why: Whole-graph compilation enables fusion that eager frameworks get only through hand-written kernels or graph capture.

questions.q: Why can kernel fusion give large speedups for chains of element-wise ops?
options: The chain is memory-bound; fusing removes intermediate reads and writes
questions.why: A chain of five element-wise ops fused into one reads and writes the data once instead of five times.

questions.q: Why must Triton block sizes be powers of two?
options: Global memory is addressed in powers of two
`tl.arange` and the compiler's layouts require power-of-two shapes
questions.why: Use masks to handle sizes that aren't a power of two.

questions.q: When is writing a custom kernel not worth it?
options: When the operation is already well served by a library call or compiler fusion, or isn't a bottleneck
questions.why: Profile first. Custom kernels add maintenance cost.

questions.q: What does an all-reduce do?
options: Combines (for example sums) a tensor across all ranks and leaves the result on every rank
Sends one rank's data to all
questions.why: It equals a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather.

questions.q: In a ring all-reduce over p ranks, how much data does each rank send?
options: The tensor size divided by p
questions.why: Reduce-scatter and all-gather each send (p − 1)/p. The cost barely grows with p, which is why rings scale well in bandwidth.

questions.q: What is effective (bus) bandwidth for a collective?
options: The data each rank must move divided by the time, which lets you compare against link bandwidth
The tensor size divided by time
questions.why: For all-reduce, bus bandwidth = (size × 2(p − 1)/p) / time.

questions.q: In data parallelism, what must happen before the optimiser step?
options: Weights are all-reduced after the step
Gradients are all-reduced (averaged) across replicas so every replica applies the same update
questions.why: Implementations overlap the all-reduce with the backward pass by bucketing gradients.

questions.q: In a column-parallel linear layer, how is the weight split?
options: Along the output dimension, so each rank computes a slice of the output features
questions.why: Following it with a row-parallel layer means only one all-reduce is needed for the pair.

questions.q: How do you reconstruct the full output from column-parallel shards?
options: Concatenate the ranks' output slices along the feature dimension (an all-gather)
questions.why: Row-parallel shards, by contrast, produce partial sums that must be added.

questions.q: What does a reduce-scatter leave on each rank?
options: One shard of the reduced result
questions.why: ZeRO and FSDP use it for gradients, so each rank only keeps the shard it updates.

questions.q: Why does data parallelism alone stop scaling for very large models?
options: Every replica must hold the full model, gradients and optimiser state, which eventually exceeds one GPU's memory
questions.why: Sharding state (ZeRO) or the model itself (tensor or pipeline parallelism) is then needed.

questions.q: What does ZeRO stage 1 shard across data-parallel ranks?
questions.why: Stage 2 also shards gradients, and stage 3 (or FSDP) also shards parameters.

questions.q: With mixed-precision Adam (16 bytes per parameter) and 8 data-parallel ranks, about how many bytes per parameter does each rank hold under ZeRO stage 3?
questions.why: All 16 bytes are sharded: 16 / 8 = 2. Parameters are gathered on demand for each layer's forward and backward.

questions.q: What is the pipeline bubble?
options: Idle time at the start and end of each step while the pipeline fills and drains
questions.why: For p stages and m micro-batches in a GPipe-style schedule, the bubble fraction is (p − 1)/(m + p − 1).

questions.q: With 4 pipeline stages and 12 micro-batches, what is the bubble fraction?
questions.why: (p − 1)/(m + p − 1) = 3/15. More micro-batches shrink the bubble but need more activation memory.

questions.q: What does a 1F1B pipeline schedule improve over GPipe?
options: Peak activation memory, since each stage starts backward passes early and holds fewer micro-batches at once
questions.why: The bubble is the same as GPipe for the same p and m. Interleaved schedules reduce it further.

questions.q: Why is tensor parallelism usually placed on the fastest links?
options: It communicates within every layer, so its collectives are on the critical path
questions.why: A typical plan is tensor parallel inside a node, pipeline across nodes and data parallel across groups.

questions.q: What does "topology-aware" mean when choosing a parallel plan?
options: Placing all GPUs in one rack
Mapping the most communication-heavy dimensions to the highest-bandwidth links between GPUs
questions.why: The same plan can be much slower if tensor-parallel groups span slow inter-node links.

questions.q: What does activation checkpointing trade?
options: Extra compute (recomputing activations in the backward pass) for lower activation memory
questions.why: Recomputing each layer's forward adds about one extra forward pass in total.

questions.q: What does a saturating power law $L(x) = E + A x^{-\alpha}$ add over a plain power law?
options: An irreducible loss floor E that the curve approaches
questions.why: Fitting without E overestimates how fast loss keeps falling at large scale.

questions.q: Why fit scaling laws in log space?
options: A pure power law is a straight line in log-log coordinates, and errors are closer to multiplicative
questions.why: With a floor, fit log(L − E) or use nonlinear least squares directly.

questions.q: What does an IsoFLOP analysis do?
options: Fixes the model and varies data only
Trains several model sizes at fixed compute and finds the size that minimises loss, then repeats across budgets
Trains one model for many FLOPs
questions.why: Fitting the optimum size against compute gives an exponent such as N_opt ∝ C^a.

questions.q: What did Chinchilla conclude about compute-optimal training?
options: Parameters and tokens should grow in roughly equal proportion, around 20 tokens per parameter
Models should be as large as possible on fixed data
Data matters more than parameters by 10×
questions.why: Many earlier models were undertrained for their size by this measure.

questions.q: What is the critical batch size?
options: The batch size beyond which larger batches give much smaller reductions in the number of steps needed
The batch where loss is zero
The largest batch that fits in memory
questions.why: Below it, doubling the batch roughly halves the steps; above it, returns diminish. It tends to grow as loss falls.

questions.q: Why are data mixture scaling curves extrapolated per domain?
options: Different domains improve at different rates with more data, so the best mixture can change with scale
questions.why: Small-scale experiments fit per-domain curves, which are then used to predict loss for a target mixture at larger scale.

questions.q: A fit gives $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.5}$. If compute grows 100×, how should model size change?
questions.why: 100^0.5 = 10. Tokens would also grow about 10× if they follow the same exponent.

questions.q: What is a risk when extrapolating a scaling law far beyond fitted points?
options: Small errors in the exponent compound, and new regimes (such as data repetition) can bend the curve
questions.why: Fit over as wide a range as possible and check predictions against at least one larger held-out run.

questions.q: During decode with a KV cache, what does attention compute for the new token?
options: Attention only to the previous token
Full attention over the whole sequence again
Scores between its query and all cached keys, then a weighted sum of cached values
questions.why: The new key and value are appended to the cache first, so the token also attends to itself.

questions.q: How do you estimate how many tokens of KV cache fit in memory?
options: Free memory after weights ÷ (2 · layers · KV heads · head dim · bytes per value)
questions.why: Divide by the expected sequence length to get the number of concurrent requests.

questions.q: In exact speculative sampling, when is draft token x accepted?
options: With probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target and q the draft distribution
Always, if it is the target's argmax
questions.why: On rejection, sample from the normalised max(0, p − q). The output distribution then equals p exactly.

questions.q: If all k draft tokens are accepted, what happens next?
options: One extra token is sampled from the target's distribution at the next position, giving k + 1 tokens for one target pass
The draft generates another k before checking
The step ends with k tokens
questions.why: The target's forward pass already produced that distribution, so the bonus token is free.

questions.q: Why is the decode phase usually memory-bandwidth bound at small batch?
options: Every step reads all weights and the KV cache to produce one token per sequence
Decoding needs more FLOPs than prefill
questions.why: Batching more sequences reuses each weight read for more tokens.

questions.q: What happens to throughput and latency as the decode batch grows?
options: Throughput rises, while per-token latency stays flat at first and then rises once compute-bound
questions.why: The knee of that curve is a natural operating point.

questions.q: Why are prompt tokens processed in parallel but output tokens one at a time?
options: Output tokens use a different model
All prompt tokens are known up front; each output token depends on the one before it
questions.why: Speculative decoding and multi-token prediction try to break this sequential dependency.

questions.q: What does a KV-cache capacity plan need besides model shape?
options: Expected sequence lengths, the concurrency target and memory reserved for activations and fragmentation
questions.why: Paged allocators reduce fragmentation but still need headroom.

questions.q: What does a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedule look like?
options: A constant rate with no warm-up
Linear warm-up, a long constant learning rate, then a short final decay
A cosine from the start to the end
questions.why: The stable phase can be branched at any point with a short decay, giving checkpoints for many training lengths from one run.

questions.q: Why is learning-rate warm-up used at the start of training?
options: To speed up the first steps
Early updates with large learning rates can be unstable while Adam's moment estimates and the weights are still poorly scaled
questions.why: Warm-up over a few thousand steps is typical.

questions.q: How do the optimal learning rate and batch size typically scale with model size?
options: Larger models usually need smaller learning rates; optimal batch size tends to grow with compute or data
questions.why: Fitting these trends on small runs lets you set hyperparameters for large runs without a full sweep.

questions.q: What does the Muon optimiser do to the momentum update for a weight matrix?
options: Sets it to the sign of the gradient
Normalises each element by its variance
Approximately orthogonalises it (for example with Newton-Schulz iterations), so all singular directions get similar step sizes
questions.why: Orthogonalisation replaces $UΣV^\top$ with roughly $UV^\top$. Embeddings and scalar parameters are usually left to AdamW.

questions.q: What problem does μP (maximal update parametrisation) solve?
options: It removes the need for an optimiser
Hyperparameters tuned on a narrow model stay near-optimal as width grows
questions.why: It rescales initialisation and per-layer learning rates with width so updates stay the same size.

questions.q: Under μP, which diagnostic should stay roughly constant as width grows?
options: The typical size of activation updates per step in each layer
questions.why: Plotting per-layer activation or update norms against width is a quick check of whether the parametrisation is correct.

questions.q: Why does a short final decay phase in WSD improve loss substantially?
options: Lowering the learning rate lets the model settle into a sharper minimum that high-rate noise kept it out of
questions.why: Most of the loss drop from annealing happens in the decay, which can be as short as 10–20% of training.

questions.q: Why fit hyperparameter scaling laws instead of sweeping at the target scale?
options: A sweep at full scale costs many full training runs; small-scale fits predict the optimum at a fraction of the cost
questions.why: The risk is that trends change at scale, so check against at least one larger run.

questions.q: What is conditional perplexity on a response?
options: The number of tokens in the response
The perplexity of prompt and response together
The perplexity of the response tokens given the prompt, with prompt tokens excluded from the average
questions.why: Mask the prompt in the loss so the metric measures only how well the model predicts the answer.

questions.q: In log-likelihood multiple-choice evaluation, why normalise by length?
options: Longer answer options have lower total log-probability simply because they have more tokens
questions.why: Common choices are per-token or per-character normalisation. Each can favour different options, so report which one was used.

questions.q: What does the Elo (Bradley-Terry) model assume about pairwise votes?
options: Every model wins half the time
Ratings are fixed by model size
The probability that A beats B is a logistic function of their rating difference
Votes are independent of the models
questions.why: P(A beats B) = σ((r_A − r_B)·ln10/400) in Elo units. Fitting by maximum likelihood is more stable than online Elo updates.

questions.q: Why is fitting Bradley-Terry ratings by maximum likelihood preferred over sequential Elo updates for leaderboards?
options: It is faster for one vote
The fit doesn't depend on the order of battles and uses all comparisons jointly
questions.why: Bootstrapping the fit gives confidence intervals.

questions.q: LLM judges tend to prefer longer responses. How can this bias be reduced?
options: Truncate every response to one sentence
Ask the judge to ignore length, with no checks
Model the score as depending on length and remove that component, or compare at matched lengths
questions.why: A regression of score on length difference estimates the bias. The adjusted score is what remains.

questions.q: Why is benchmark contamination a problem?
options: If test items appear in training data, scores measure memorisation instead of ability
questions.why: n-gram overlap checks between training data and test sets are a common defence.

questions.q: What does pass@k measure for code generation?
options: The probability that at least one of k sampled solutions passes the tests
The fraction of tests passed by one sample
questions.why: The unbiased estimator draws n ≥ k samples, counts c correct ones, and computes 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k).

questions.q: Why should evaluation prompts and formatting be fixed across models being compared?
options: Small changes in prompt wording or few-shot examples can shift scores by several points
questions.why: Report the exact template and decoding settings with results.

questions.q: What does stable exact deduplication keep?
options: The first occurrence of each duplicate, in original order
questions.why: Hashing normalised documents makes it linear time. "Stable" means the order of kept documents doesn't change.

questions.q: Why does near-duplicate removal use MinHash and LSH rather than pairwise comparison?
options: Comparing all pairs is quadratic; LSH buckets likely duplicates so only a few pairs are checked
LSH removes all duplicates without hashing
questions.why: Banding r rows per band over b bands gives an S-curve that sets the similarity threshold.

questions.q: In temperature-based data mixing with weights $p_i \propto n_i^{1/T}$, what does T > 1 do?
options: Upsamples smaller sources relative to their natural size
questions.why: T = 1 uses natural proportions; large T approaches a uniform mix. Multilingual models use it to give low-resource languages more weight.

questions.q: Why is deduplication important for pretraining?
options: It is only needed for code
Repeated text wastes compute, encourages memorisation and can skew the model toward boilerplate
questions.why: Dedup also reduces the chance of benchmark items appearing many times.

questions.q: What is a risk of over-upsampling a small, high-quality source?
options: The model sees the same examples many times and starts to overfit or memorise them
questions.why: Beyond a few epochs, repeated data gives diminishing and then negative returns.

questions.q: What do quality filters such as perplexity or classifier scores aim to remove?
options: Low-quality text such as spam, boilerplate and machine-generated junk
questions.why: Filters can also remove useful dialects or topics, so their effects should be audited.

questions.q: When computing MinHash, what is the shingle?
options: A short contiguous sequence of words or characters used as a set element
questions.why: Choosing 5-word shingles, for example, makes small edits change only a few elements of the set.

questions.q: Why must data mixtures be decided before training rather than adjusted freely?
options: The learning-rate schedule and token budget interact with the mixture; changing it mid-run shifts what the model learns
questions.why: Some recipes deliberately change the mixture in a final annealing phase, which is planned up front.

questions.q: In supervised fine-tuning on chat data, why mask the loss on user turns?
options: The model should learn to produce assistant replies, not to imitate user messages
It is required by the tokenizer
questions.why: Only assistant tokens (often including the end-of-turn token) contribute to the loss.

questions.q: Why is the end-of-turn token usually included in the SFT loss?
options: So the model learns when to stop generating
questions.why: Without it, the model may keep generating past the end of a reply.

questions.q: What should canonicalising pairwise preference data handle?
options: Duplicates, contradictory pairs, ties and consistent chosen/rejected ordering
questions.why: The same pair labelled both ways gives no signal and adds noise to training.

questions.q: What is a KL-regularised policy objective?
options: The SFT loss plus the reward
questions.why: Its optimum is $\pi^*(y|x) \propto \pi_{ref}(y|x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)$, which is the starting point for DPO.

questions.q: How is the per-sequence KL to the reference estimated from samples?
options: As the sum over tokens of $\log\pi(y_t) - \log\pi_{ref}(y_t)$ on sequences sampled from π
As the difference in loss on the prompt
questions.why: This is unbiased but noisy. Lower-variance estimators exist, such as $(r - 1) - \log r$ with $r = \pi_{ref}/\pi$.

questions.q: What does the DPO loss increase during training?
options: The margin between the policy's log-ratio (to the reference) on chosen versus rejected responses
The absolute probability of the chosen response only
questions.why: Both log-probabilities can fall while the margin grows, which is a known DPO behaviour.

questions.q: What is mid-training?
options: A phase between pretraining and post-training that shifts the data mix toward higher-quality or targeted data, often with longer contexts
Training at half the learning rate
questions.why: It is often combined with the learning-rate decay at the end of pretraining.

questions.q: Why do post-training recipes often start from SFT before preference optimisation?
options: The model must first follow the chat format and produce reasonable answers for preferences to refine
Preference methods can't use base models at all
SFT removes the need for preferences
questions.why: Preference methods compare responses; they work best when both responses are already plausible.

questions.q: What does RLVR stand for?
questions.why: The reward comes from a checker, such as unit tests or an answer match, rather than a learned reward model.

questions.q: In GRPO, how is each response's advantage computed?
options: (reward − mean of the group's rewards) ÷ standard deviation of the group's rewards
questions.why: Responses to the same prompt form the group.

questions.q: What happens to GRPO advantages when every response in a group gets the same reward?
options: They become undefined and training crashes
They are all zero (with an ε in the denominator), so the prompt gives no gradient
questions.why: Prompts that are always solved or never solved carry no signal. Filtering them saves compute.

questions.q: How does sequence-level length normalisation differ from token-level normalisation in the policy loss?
options: Sequence-level averages each response's token losses first, so long responses get less weight per token; token-level averages over all tokens
questions.why: Sequence-level weighting can bias the model toward longer wrong answers or shorter right ones.

questions.q: Why might standardising by group standard deviation cause problems?
options: Groups with nearly identical rewards get their small differences amplified, giving too much weight to easy or hard prompts
questions.why: Some variants use only mean-centring, without the division.

questions.q: Why is a verifiable reward less prone to reward hacking than a learned reward model?
options: It can't be gamed at all
It checks the actual outcome, so there is no learned model whose errors the policy can exploit
questions.why: Verifiers can still be gamed, for example by tests that are too weak or answers formatted to fool the parser.

questions.q: Why sample several responses per prompt in GRPO?
options: To pick the best one for SFT
The group provides the baseline that replaces a learned value function
To increase the batch size only
questions.why: Typical group sizes are 4 to 64.

questions.q: What does a pass-rate curriculum do in RLVR?
options: Trains on the easiest prompts only
Focuses training on prompts the model solves sometimes but not always, where the gradient signal is strongest
Trains on the hardest prompts only
questions.why: Pass rates shift as the model improves, so the pool is refreshed during training.

questions.q: How does a ViT turn an image into tokens?
options: Run a language model on the pixels
Split it into fixed-size patches, flatten each patch, and project it linearly
questions.why: A 224×224 image with 14×14 patches gives 256 tokens.

questions.q: What does CLIP's symmetric contrastive loss do?
options: Regresses image embeddings onto text embeddings
Treats each matched image-text pair as the correct class in a softmax over the batch, in both image-to-text and text-to-image directions
questions.why: The two cross-entropy losses are averaged. A learned temperature scales the cosine similarities.

questions.q: How does SigLIP's loss differ from CLIP's?
options: It uses a larger temperature only
It uses an independent sigmoid on every image-text pair instead of a softmax over the batch
questions.why: No normalisation across the batch is needed, which simplifies large distributed batches. A learned bias offsets the many negatives.

questions.q: Why does SigLIP need a bias term in its logits?
options: Most pairs are negatives, so without a bias the loss would be dominated by pushing negatives down at the start
questions.why: The bias starts strongly negative so initial predictions match the heavy class imbalance.

questions.q: In a vision-language model, how are image tokens usually combined with text?
options: They are summed into the first token only
Image patch embeddings are projected into the language model's embedding space and placed in the token sequence
They are used only by the output layer
questions.why: A projector (often an MLP) maps vision features to the LM's hidden size.

questions.q: What does multimodal RoPE (such as M-RoPE) do for image tokens?
options: Assigns separate position components for time, height and width so the model knows each patch's 2-D location
Uses the same position for every image token
questions.why: Text tokens use the same value for all components, so they behave like ordinary 1-D RoPE.

questions.q: Why does the batch size matter so much in contrastive pretraining?
options: Each example's negatives are the other examples in the batch, so larger batches give more and harder negatives
Small batches are faster to converge
Large batches remove the need for temperature
questions.why: CLIP used a batch of 32,768.

questions.q: What is a common alignment failure in vision-language models?
options: Describing objects that aren't in the image (hallucination), often driven by language priors
questions.why: Preference training and grounding data are common mitigations.

questions.q: In continuous decode batching, when does a new request join the running batch?
options: At the next iteration boundary, as soon as a slot and enough KV memory are free
Only when the whole batch has finished
questions.why: Iteration-level scheduling keeps the GPU full as requests finish at different times.

questions.q: What does a KV-cache trie (prefix tree) let a server find?
options: The longest cached prefix shared between a new request and earlier requests
questions.why: Matching on token IDs means the cached keys and values for that prefix can be reused.

questions.q: What does cache-aware routing do in a multi-replica deployment?
options: Sends a request to the replica most likely to have its prefix cached, while still balancing load
Duplicates every request on all replicas
Sends every request to the least-loaded replica only
questions.why: Pure cache affinity can overload one replica, so routers mix the two goals.

questions.q: What does a kernel timeline utilisation measure show?
options: The FLOP/s of the fastest kernel
The fraction of wall-clock time the GPU spends running kernels, which exposes gaps from launch overhead or CPU stalls
questions.why: Small decode kernels can leave large gaps between launches. CUDA graphs or fused kernels reduce them.

questions.q: Why do CUDA graphs help small-batch decoding?
options: They record a sequence of kernel launches and replay it with one launch, removing per-kernel CPU overhead
questions.why: At small batch, kernels are short enough that launch overhead is a large share of step time.

questions.q: Why can prefix reuse dramatically reduce time to first token?
options: The prefill for the shared prefix is skipped, so only the new suffix must be processed
questions.why: Long system prompts or multi-turn chats benefit most.

questions.q: When should a cached prefix be evicted?
options: When memory is needed, usually choosing least-recently-used entries that no running request references
questions.why: Blocks still used by active requests must be pinned.

questions.q: What is the main cost of keeping many cached prefixes?
options: They take GPU memory that could otherwise hold more concurrent requests' KV caches
questions.why: The best cache size balances hit rate against admission capacity.
